### **Live Synthesis | GridPulse AI Insights**

Scotland’s transmission network is currently exhibiting the classic tension between high-yield renewable generation and structural grid architecture. Regional wind generation has surged to an exceptional **4,350.8 MW**, driving regional carbon intensity down to an ultra-clean **32 gCO2/kWh**. 

However, this clean power surge is severely testing the transmission limits of the **Cheviot boundary (B6 interface)**. Physical cross-border thermal transfer capacity is actively saturated, preventing surplus zero-marginal-cost generation from flowing south to primary English demand centres. To preserve network frequency and thermal safety, the Electricity System Operator (ESO) is enforcing bid-offer curtailment on northern assets while redispatching more expensive, flexible generation south of the constraint.

With constraint cost factors currently elevated at **£135/MWh**, this locational imbalance carries steep financial consequences. The friction of paying generators both to ramp down in the north and ramp up in the south flows directly into **Balancing Services Use of System (BSUoS)** charges. Ultimately, these network inefficiencies create acute economic pressures on end-consumers, translating high wind yields into elevated systemic retail levies until planned cross-border subsea links and inland transmission reinforcements reach commissioning.
